lead: A column that carries axial load and bending must be checked as one combined problem. The interaction diagram plots factored axial load Pu against factored moment Mu. Every point inside the curve is a safe load-moment pair for that section and steel. For bending about both axes, two uniaxial capacities are used in a load contour check. Designers use this for building columns, bridge piers and industrial frames, where loads are rarely perfectly centred.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for short and slender columns, 5.2 for axial capacity, and Unit 1 for partial safety factors and stress block parameters.

blocks.text: Pu is the factored axial load in kN. Mu is the factored moment in kN·m about the axis being checked. A short column section has a limit curve in the Pu-Mu plane. The curve is the interaction diagram.

The curve has three landmarks. At pure compression, M<sub>u</sub> is zero and P<sub>u</sub> is largest. At the balanced point, concrete reaches its limit strain and steel yields at the same time. At pure bending, P<sub>u</sub> is zero and the section carries only M<sub>u</sub>. Between these points the curve bends inward. Any load-moment pair inside the curve is safe; any pair outside is unsafe.

Design charts, such as SP 16, give M<sub>ux1</sub> for a chosen section, steel percentage and concrete grade at a given P<sub>u</sub>. Read M<sub>ux1</sub> on the horizontal axis and P<sub>u</sub> on the vertical axis. The chart already uses factored loads and limit state material strengths. Do not mix service loads with chart values.
e<sub>min</sub> = l/500 + D/30, with e<sub>min</sub> ≥ 20 mm
blocks.where: e<sub>min</sub> is the minimum eccentricity in mm; l is the unsupported length in mm; D is the lateral dimension in the plane of bending in mm.

blocks.text: Real columns are never perfectly axial. The minimum moment is P<sub>u</sub> e<sub>min</sub>. Add it to the calculated moment in that axis before reading the chart. This covers unavoidable load eccentricity and construction tolerance.

sections.h3: Biaxial bending and the load contour

blocks.text: Biaxial bending means moment about both principal axes at once. Corner columns and columns in frames under wind or earthquake commonly have M<sub>ux</sub> and M<sub>uy</sub> together. A uniaxial check on each axis alone is not enough.

blocks.where: M<sub>ux</sub> and M<sub>uy</sub> are applied factored moments about the x and y axes in kN·m. M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> are the uniaxial moment capacities about the same axes at the same P<sub>u</sub>, in kN·m. αn is the load contour exponent, usually between 1 and 2.

blocks.text: For a fixed P<sub>u</sub>, the safe biaxial capacity is a curve in the M<sub>ux</sub>-M<sub>uy</sub> plane. The exponent αn shapes this curve. αn near 1 gives a straight line; αn near 2 gives a rounded contour. At low axial load use a value nearer 1; at high axial load use a value nearer 2, or take the value from the code or chart.

The method is often called the Bresler load contour method. Use M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> read at the same P<sub>u</sub>. Do not use the pure moment capacity or the capacity at a different axial load.

items: Compute factored P<sub>u</sub> and the factored moments M<sub>ux</sub> and M<sub>uy</sub>, including the minimum eccentricity moment in each axis.
Choose a trial section and longitudinal steel. Read M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> from SP 16 at the same P<sub>u</sub>.
Check each axis alone: M<sub>ux</sub> ≤ M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy</sub> ≤ M<sub>uy1</sub>.
Check the biaxial load contour with the specified αn.
If the contour sum is greater than 1, increase the section or the steel and repeat.

blocks.text: Rectangular column charts are normalized. The axes are P<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub> b D) and M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub> b D²), and the curve parameter is p/f<sub>ck</sub>, where f<sub>ck</sub> is the concrete grade in N/mm², b and D are the section dimensions in mm, and p is the steel percentage. Choose the chart for the concrete grade and bar layout, then convert back using the actual b and D. Circular column charts use the ratio of steel area to gross area; a symmetric circular section has the same uniaxial moment capacity about any diameter. Check steel percentage limits and tie detailing from Unit 3.

If one moment dominates, compare each applied moment with its uniaxial capacity first. If either ratio exceeds 1, the section fails before the biaxial check. The contour check then decides the combined case.
Slender columns add second-order moment. Effective length and slenderness are in 5.1. A short column ignores second-order effects, but it does not ignore minimum eccentricity.

figure.caption: The curve is the section's limit for axial load and moment. The design point at 90 kN·m and 800 kN lies inside, so the section is safe.

spec.aria: Interaction curve of axial load against moment; the design point at 90 kN·m and 800 kN lies inside the curve.

examples.question: A 300 mm × 400 mm short column has 4 bars of 20 mm diameter, M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. It carries Pu = 800 kN, Mux = 90 kN·m and Muy = 40 kN·m. From SP 16 charts, Mux1 = 130 kN·m and Muy1 = 100 kN·m at Pu. Check the section for biaxial bending using αn = 1.5.
steps: Write the data: b = 300 mm, D = 400 mm, P<sub>u</sub> = 800 kN, M<sub>ux</sub> = 90 kN·m, M<sub>uy</sub> = 40 kN·m, M<sub>ux1</sub> = 130 kN·m, M<sub>uy1</sub> = 100 kN·m, αn = 1.5.
Assume the given moments already include the minimum eccentricity moment. If not, add P<sub>u</sub> e<sub>min</sub> to each axis first.
Steel area: A<sub>sc</sub> = 4 × π × 20²/4 = 1256.6 mm². This is about 1.05% of 300 × 400 mm², which matches the chart steel percentage.
0.829 ≤ 1.0, so the section passes the biaxial load contour check.
examples.answer: The column is safe for biaxial bending; the interaction sum is 0.829 ≤ 1.0.
examples.check:
Mux = 90.0
Muy = 40.0
Mux1 = 130.0
Muy1 = 100.0
an = 1.5
rx = (Mux / Mux1) ** an
ry = (Muy / Muy1) ** an
s = rx + ry
print(f"{rx:.3f}")
print(f"{ry:.3f}")
print(f"{s:.3f}")

traps: Adding the two moment ratios linearly when αn is not 1. The code check uses each ratio raised to αn.
Reading M<sub>ux1</sub> or M<sub>uy1</sub> at a different P<sub>u</sub>, or using service moments instead of factored moments.
Forgetting the minimum eccentricity moment P<sub>u</sub> e<sub>min</sub> before the chart is read.
Using the uniaxial capacity about the wrong axis, or swapping b and D in the chart.
Treating a slender column's first-order moment as final; second-order effects belong with effective length in 5.1.

quiz.q: What two quantities does a column interaction diagram plot?
quiz.a: Factored axial load P<sub>u</sub> on the vertical axis and factored moment M<sub>u</sub> on the horizontal axis.

quiz.q: Why is a load-moment point inside the interaction curve safe?
quiz.a: The section capacity curve lies outside it, so the applied P<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>u</sub> are below the section's limit in that direction.

quiz.q: For a column, M<sub>ux</sub>/M<sub>ux1</sub> = 0.60 and M<sub>uy</sub>/M<sub>uy1</sub> = 0.50. Check biaxial bending for αn = 1.5.
Why must M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> be read at the same P<sub>u</sub> as the design axial load?
quiz.a: M<sub>ux1</sub> is not constant; it changes with P<sub>u</sub>. It rises as P<sub>u</sub> increases up to the balanced point and falls beyond it. So capacities read at another P<sub>u</sub> describe a different load contour and give a wrong check.

quiz.q: Name the three key points on a column interaction curve.
quiz.a: Pure compression, balanced point and pure bending.

quiz.q: A column has P<sub>u</sub> = 1000 kN, M<sub>ux1</sub> = 150 kN·m, M<sub>uy1</sub> = 120 kN·m, M<sub>ux</sub> = 60 kN·m and M<sub>uy</sub> = 60 kN·m. Check for αn = 2.0.
What is the minimum eccentricity moment and why is it used?
quiz.a: It is P<sub>u</sub> e<sub>min</sub>, with e<sub>min</sub> = l/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm. It covers unavoidable load eccentricity and construction tolerance.

quiz.q: A linear sum M<sub>ux</sub>/M<sub>ux1</sub> + M<sub>uy</sub>/M<sub>uy1</sub> = 1.05 is used to reject a section for αn = 1.5. Is rejection always correct?
quiz.a: No. For αn > 1 the exponent sum can be below the linear sum. Example: 0.60<sup>1.5</sup> + 0.45<sup>1.5</sup> = 0.465 + 0.302 = 0.767 ≤ 1, so the section may pass. Use the specified exponent check.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial software represents the full interaction surface as a mesh of P<sub>u</sub>, M<sub>ux</sub> and M<sub>uy</sub> values, and checks each factored load combination against it. Fibre section analysis computes the surface directly from concrete and steel stress-strain curves, including confinement and high-strength materials. Newer codes keep the same load contour idea but calibrate the exponent with test data. Search for Bresler load contour, biaxial bending interaction surface, and fibre section analysis of RC columns.
